items.title: Putin proposes humanitarian mission in eastern Ukraine during talks with U.S. envoys
text: MOSCOW, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday proposed organizing a humanitarian mission to evacuate civilians from Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine, drawing on previous experience in Oleshky.

Speaking during talks in Moscow with U.S. presidential special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, Putin said hundreds of civilians remained in the city and called for their evacuation.
Located in the Donetsk region, Kostiantynivka had served as a key Ukrainian military stronghold. Russia claimed to have taken full control of the city in July.

On territorial issues, Putin said Russia would recognize "only the state border" as the line of demarcation with Ukraine. He reiterated Moscow's opposition to the deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine, warning that such forces would pose a threat to Russia's national security and become legitimate military targets.

Putin also said Moscow has never opposed dialogue with Europe, but European countries has severed contacts with Russia. He expressed hope that Washington would work with European countries to promote peace, and stressed the need for a lasting settlement of the Ukraine conflict.

Russian forces continued strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial and energy facilities using ground-based precision-guided weapons and long-range attack drones, the Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday.

Russian forces struck drone production and assembly plants in Kiev and the surrounding region, as well as facilities in the Kiev region producing solid rocket fuel components for operational-tactical missiles and solid-fuel boosters for drones, it said.

On the same day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would never recognize Russia's occupation of its territories, regardless of any decision made by the United States, the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported.

"We must make it clear that we will never, under any circumstances, recognize Russia's occupation of Ukrainian territory," Zelensky told the plenary session of the European Political Community summit.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine could not agree to withdraw from the Donbas region to end the conflict, because the issue concerns the country's independence.  ■

items.title: Xi Focus: Xi calls for carrying forward Sun Yat-sen's legacy in national rejuvenation drive
text: Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, addresses a gathering to commemorate the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei)

BEIJING, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for carrying forward the legacy of Sun Yat-sen, one of the nation's revered revolutionary forefathers, to make joint efforts for national rejuvenation and turn into reality the great dream of all Chinese people since the advent of modern times.

Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a gathering held in Beijing to commemorate the 160th anniversary of Sun's birth.
Born in 1866, Sun led the Revolution of 1911 more than a century ago to abolish the absolute monarchy that had ruled China for thousands of years. Sun died in 1925.

Thursday's gathering in the Great Hall of the People was attended by about 3,000 people, including senior Chinese leaders Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee. Wang presided over the event.
Xi met with Sun's relatives and representatives of overseas guests before the event started.
In his speech, Xi hailed Sun as a great national hero, a great patriot and a great pioneer of China's democratic revolution.
He said that Chinese communists are the most steadfast supporters, loyal collaborators, and faithful successors to the revolutionary cause initiated by Sun.
For more than 100 years, the CPC has led the Chinese people in writing the most magnificent chapter in the history of the Chinese nation, Xi said.
"The best way for us to remember Dr. Sun is to emulate, inherit and carry forward his invaluable spirit, steadily advancing our endeavors to build a great country and rejuvenate our nation," Xi said.
Highlighting Sun's lifelong devotion to the country, Xi called on all Chinese people to learn from Sun and promote patriotism to strive for a strong and prosperous China.
He also lauded Sun's dedication to the people, underscoring the imperative of always putting the people first and serving them wholeheartedly.
On the new journey, it is essential to make solid headway in promoting well-rounded personal development and common prosperity for all, Xi stressed.

Noting that Sun devoted his life to the pursuit of truth, Xi stressed the need to learn from Sun's example, advance theoretical exploration and innovation with courage, and continue to write new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of the times.
Xi called on the Chinese people to carry forward Sun's unyielding determination, rise to challenges ahead and break new ground in the country's development.

"We must carry forward the fighting spirit, build up our ability, be ready to withstand high winds, choppy waters, and even dangerous storms, and overcome all the risks and challenges we face on the way forward," Xi said.

items.title: In China's Ningxia, medical aid flows in and out via telemedicine
text: YINCHUAN, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- At a health center in Minning Town, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, a recent video consultation connected doctors more than 2,000 kilometers apart for real-time medical guidance.

Yao Li, a physician sent from coastal Fujian Province to Ningxia last year under a government-led east-west medical assistance program, was consulting specialists at Fujian's Xiamen Children's Hospital about a seven-month-old baby with epilepsy. After reviewing the infant's medical records and imaging results, they worked out a treatment plan together, sparing the family a long trip for specialist care.
"We were particularly worried about traveling so far with such a young child," one of the parents said. "We didn't expect specialists in Xiamen could help us work out a plan right here."

For Ningxia, reaching patients in remote areas has long been a challenge. To bridge the gap, the region has increasingly turned to digital healthcare. Such service allows patients to undergo examinations at local health centers while specialists at larger hospitals review their results remotely.

In 2018, Ningxia was approved to develop China's first "Internet Plus Healthcare" pilot area. Since then, it has built a remote medical network linking hospitals and health centers across five administrative levels, extending down to townships.

Behind Ningxia's expanding healthcare network lies a long history of medical cooperation. Since 1996, coastal Fujian Province has sent more than 1,500 medical specialists to the region. But Ningxia has not remained merely a recipient of assistance. It has also dispatched its own medical teams overseas, extending medical expertise beyond China's borders.

Ningxia sent its first medical team to Benin on Jan. 8, 1978. Since then, it has dispatched 28 teams to the country, involving more than 660 medical personnel. Together, they have provided over 3 million patient consultations and performed more than 75,000 operations.

Now, Chinese doctors working overseas are increasingly drawing on an approach that has proved effective at home: using technology, including telemedicine, to bring specialist care to patients far from major hospitals.

In March 2019, Chinese doctors in Benin performed the first operation in the history of China's overseas medical aid program with remote video guidance. More than 10 medical specialists from Ningxia provided real-time advice through a video link from over 10,000 kilometers away, spending nearly five hours guiding the surgical team as it removed a large thyroid tumor from a local patient.

A telemedicine platform launched in 2023 allows Chinese medical teams in Benin to consult specialists back in China while providing treatment locally, bringing expertise across borders without requiring patients to travel long distances.

Ma Yan, a traditional Chinese medicine specialist serving in Benin, recently used the system to consult colleagues in Ningxia about a 73-year-old patient whose left side had been weakened by cerebrovascular disease.

items.title: China, U.S. hold political dialogue in Beijing
text: BEIJING, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- A senior Chinese official said candid, in-depth and constructive views were exchanged at the U.S.-China Political Dialogue 2026 held in Beijing Thursday, under the theme of "U.S.-China Relations in the New Era: Exploring the Right Approach in a Changing Asia-Pacific and the World."

Liu Haixing, head of the International Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that a stable, sound and sustainable China-U.S. relationship not only serves the interests of the two peoples, but also provides an important guarantee for peace and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific and the world.

He called on the two sides to uphold the principles of mutual respect, peaceful coexistence and win-win cooperation, work together to explore the right way for the two major countries to get along in the new era, and jointly consolidate the foundation for a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.

The U.S. representatives noted that U.S.-China relations are at an important juncture. They called for strengthening dialogue and exchanges, expanding mutually beneficial cooperation, and working for the long-term, stable and sound development of U.S.-China relations, to inject stability and development momentum into the Asia-Pacific and the world.

The event was attended by representatives from U.S. political parties, the strategic and business community, and from relevant Chinese government departments, local governments, think tanks, universities and civil society organizations.

items.title: Budapest conference highlights RMB's growing role in trade, financing
text: Guests attend a panel discussion during the 10th Budapest Renminbi Initiative Conference in Budapest, Hungary, on Nov. 12, 2026. Themed "The Role of Renminbi in the International Monetary System," the conference was jointly organized by Hungary's central bank and Bank of China CEE Ltd. The annual forum is part of the Budapest Renminbi Initiative, launched by the central bank in 2015 to promote RMB use in Hungary and strengthen financial ties with China. (Xinhua/Hu Zhixuan)

BUDAPEST, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- The renminbi (RMB) is broadening financing options for banks and businesses engaged in trade and investment between China and Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), participants said Thursday at the 10th Budapest Renminbi Initiative Conference.
Themed "The Role of Renminbi in the International Monetary System," the conference was jointly organized by Hungary's central bank and Bank of China CEE Ltd.
The annual forum is part of the Budapest Renminbi Initiative, launched by the central bank in 2015 to promote RMB use in Hungary and strengthen financial ties with China.
Hungarian central bank Governor Mihaly Varga said the global financial system was becoming more multipolar, with regional financial networks gaining importance.
Cross-border RMB receipts and payments totaled 70.6 trillion yuan (10.57 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up 10.1 percent year-on-year, according to the People's Bank of China.
"There is no doubt that the RMB will play a very important role in the world economy of the future," Varga said.

In an interview with Xinhua, central bank Deputy Governor Daniel Palotai said the initiative aimed to facilitate wider RMB use in financial transactions as more Chinese companies and banks operated in Hungary.
"Hungary wants to serve as a bridge between the East and the West in this regard," Palotai said.

Chinese battery maker CATL and electric vehicle manufacturer BYD are among the companies investing in Hungary. Chinese companies' planned and implemented investment projects in Hungary were worth more than 26 billion euros (28.8 billion dollars), with over 30,000 jobs created, according to Chinese Ambassador to Hungary Gong Tao.

Gong also highlighted financial cooperation projects, including the launch of Central and Eastern Europe's first RMB clearing bank in Hungary in 2015 and Hungary's cumulative issuance of 11 billion yuan (1.65 billion dollars) in sovereign panda bonds.

Laszlo Bencsik, deputy CEO and chief strategic and financial officer of Hungary's OTP Bank, said the bank had raised 3.5 billion yuan (525 million dollars) through agreements with major Chinese banks and a dim sum bond issuance over the past few years, helping diversify its funding sources.
He said companies earning RMB revenues from exports to China could borrow in the same currency to hedge currency risks. "It has to come as a natural demand from clients," Bencsik said.

Yu Wenjian, head of the Shanghai Head Office of the People's Bank of China, said RMB use was expanding beyond trade settlement to financing, investment, pricing and reserves. China would further open its financial markets and improve cross-border payment services, he said.

items.title: China-Africa photo exhibition deepens friendship, cultural ties
text: Guests visit the China-Africa Impressions Photography Exhibition in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, Nov. 12, 2026. China-Africa Impressions Photography Exhibition opened Thursday here showcasing cultural ties, people-to-people exchanges and time-honored friendship between China and Africa. Held at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), the photography exhibition featured 64 photographs, which were selected from 283 entries submitted by 151 photographers of 26 nationalities. (Xinhua/Geng Xinning)

ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- China-Africa Impressions Photography Exhibition opened Thursday in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, showcasing cultural ties, people-to-people exchanges and time-honored friendship between China and Africa.

Held at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), the photography exhibition featured 64 photographs, which were selected from 283 entries submitted by 151 photographers of 26 nationalities.

The photographs were captured in more than 30 African countries and China. 24 of them won awards for uniquely depicting the diversity of China and Africa, demonstrating their development, achievements, rich cultural heritage, wildlife and landscapes.

Opening the exhibition, Jiang Feng, head of the Chinese Mission to the African Union, said the photography exhibition is a vivid example of China-Africa joint efforts to implement the Global Civilization Initiative that calls for respect for the diversity of civilizations, stronger international people-to-people exchanges, and inclusive coexistence and mutual learning.

"The exhibition provides an opportunity to further deepen mutual understanding and friendship between the peoples of China and Africa, enable exchanges among civilizations to transcend barriers, and bring our peoples closer across mountains and seas, thus laying a stronger and more enduring foundation of public support for China-Africa friendship," Jiang said.

Noting that the China-Africa friendship has a long history and has grown stronger over time, Jiang hopes that the exhibition will open new opportunities to enhance mutual understanding between the peoples of China and Africa, deepen their cultural exchanges and help build an all-weather China-Africa community with a shared future.

Mama Keita, deputy executive secretary for programme support at the UNECA, said the photographs showcase everyday moments, bringing together places, cultures and perspectives in a shared visual dialogue, honoring both distinctiveness and common humanity.

"I hope these photographs will inspire conversation, broaden our perspectives and encourage us to see our diverse cultures, experiences and heritage with fresh eyes while discovering the common ground that connects China and Africa," she said.

The event, co-organized by the Chinese Mission to the African Union and the UNECA, attracted nearly 200 guests. It also came as the two sides celebrate the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges.

items.title: Stelios Virvidakis: A lifelong dialogue between Greek and Chinese philosophy
text: The National and Kapodistrian University of Athens is one of the oldest higher education institutions in modern Greece. Stelios Virvidakis is professor emeritus of moral philosophy and epistemology and has long been an advocate for the comparative study of Greek and Chinese philosophy. "Philosophers express the self-consciousness of a culture," Virvidakis said. For him, comparative philosophy offers not only a way for Greece and China to learn from each other, but also an approach through which other cultures can enrich one another.
Stelios Virvidakis (Photo/Patrick Shead-Simmonds)

Virvidakis' interest in comparative philosophy dates back to his time as a student. Although specializing in Western philosophy, he always felt that there was something missing if alternative approaches to knowledge were not considered. "Chinese philosophy is one of the greatest traditions," he remarked. "So naturally I was curious and wanted to learn more." Since 2011, Virvidakis has frequently travelled to China to deliver lectures and seminars on topics ranging from Greek philosophy to history and culture. His first trip to China was to attend a conference hosted by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in Beijing.

Virvidakis has found many parallels between early Chinese and Greek thought. "There is a parallel between Taoism and the Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher Heraclitus," he shared. Both traditions explore a world in flux and the relationship between opposites. Virvidakis' favorite Taoist thinker is Zhuangzi, whose use of humor and paradox reminds him of the sceptics of the Hellenistic period.

In 2021, the Center of Greek and Chinese Ancient Civilisations was established. It was a joint venture between four Greek universities: the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the University of Crete, and the University of Patras. Around the same time, a counterpart was founded in China by Southwest University, Renmin University, Sichuan University, and Shandong University. Virvidakis was the first president of the Greek center and currently serves as its general secretary.

"Although there have been international centers for comparative study, this is the first Sino-Greek collaboration," Virvidakis said. "It is a bilateral effort to establish direct channels of communication through knowledge exchange." Recently, the center organized a talk on the circulation of philosophical texts from Europe to China, focusing particularly on the introduction of Aristotle to China and its subsequent transmission to Japan and Korea. Besides exploring the historical dissemination of Aristotelian philosophy in China in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the talk also examined Aristotle's reception in contemporary China.

items.title: Cartoon commentary | Hidden malice
text: The Japanese TV drama "VIVANT," which Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi publicly singled out as a series she wanted to watch, has sparked strong backlash on Chinese social media for its grossly distorted portrayal of China.

The drama features torture scenes bearing disturbing similarities to atrocities committed by Japanese troops during their invasion of China. Even more astonishing, Japanese Self-Defense Forces intelligence personnel are portrayed as "victims" and Chinese people as brutal "perpetrators."

The plot twists history and shifts the blame, but historical evidence speaks for itself. Attempts to smear China and distort the truth cannot erase the facts. This insidious form of "cultural poisoning" is both absurd and shameless, exposing the dangerous agenda of Japan's right-wing forces. The international community must remain vigilant and see through such attempts to manipulate historical memory.

items.title: Volunteers play a growing role in China's public-interest litigation
text:
By YANG ZEKUN | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-13 17:26

From uncovering environmental damage to holding authorities accountable for incomplete repairs, volunteers are taking on a greater role in China's public-interest litigation system, as six cases released by the country's top procuratorate on Friday demonstrate how public involvement can strengthen legal oversight.

The Supreme People's Procuratorate said the cases, covering environmental protection, food and drug safety, and accessibility, illustrate how volunteers can help prosecutors identify violations, provide technical expertise and monitor corrective action.

The release comes a week after China's top legislature adopted a new public-interest litigation law on Nov 6. Set to take effect on Jan 1, the law explicitly encourages organizations and individuals to help protect public interests and oversee litigation proceedings.

All six cases involved administrative public-interest litigation aimed at ensuring government agencies fulfill their legal responsibilities. Three were resolved through pre-litigation recommendations, while the remaining proceeded to court after authorities failed to address the problems adequately.

One case began in July 2024, when volunteer Cheng Zhihui alerted prosecutors in Yi'an county, Northeast China's Heilongjiang province, to severe erosion threatening the region's fertile black-soil farmland.
Investigators found that expanding gullies had destroyed more than 20,000 square meters of cropland and washed away over 60,000 cubic meters of soil, undermining local agricultural production.

Cheng joined two other volunteers with agricultural and water-management expertise to assess the damage. When the local water affairs authority failed to complete the promised restoration, the volunteers conducted six follow-up inspections, uncovering further erosion and a newly formed gully.

Their findings helped prosecutors bring an administrative lawsuit in May 2026, prompting the authority to invest 1.35 million yuan ($202,400) in restoration work, including slope stabilization, replanting and waste removal.
A subsequent independent assessment confirmed that soil erosion intensity had fallen by 95 percent, and the court concluded proceedings in August.
The SPP said its "Yixin Weigong" volunteer platform, launched in late 2020, had registered more than 100,000 volunteers across over 10 professional fields by October 2026.

Volunteers have submitted more than 42,700 reports of suspected harm to public interests and participated in more than 72,600 case-related activities, including expert consultations, hearings and follow-up inspections.

The procuratorate said it plans to establish specialized volunteer teams and improve procedures for reporting violations, providing expert advice and monitoring corrective measures, seeking to make public participation a more systematic part of public-interest litigation.

items.title: Huang's exit puts Nvidia leadership, AI policy in focus
text: Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy.

Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement.

The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman.
Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion.

The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily.

"Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power.
He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations.

The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership.
The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China.

Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China.
Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift.
"AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report.

Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed.

items.title: Remy Cointreau turns to AI, younger consumers to drive growth
text:
By WANG ZHUOQIONG | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-13 09:41

The artificial intelligence-powered sales presenter for French spirits maker Remy Cointreau can introduce cognac and whisky to Chinese shoppers at 3 am, answering questions and recommending products long after her human colleagues have signed off.

The virtual host, Eve, introduced about 18 months ago, is part of the company's push to expand its digital reach and attract new customers, as China's premium spirits market shifts away from traditional business banquets toward more personal drinking occasions.

"There's very little overlap," said Sophie Phe, CEO of Remy Cointreau China, of the audiences reached by AI and human livestreaming presenters during an interview at the just-concluded ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai.

Human presenters still account for about 80 percent of the company's livestreaming activity, compared with 20 percent for AI-powered sessions. While human hosts continue to deliver stronger commercial results, the technology allows Remy Cointreau to reach consumers around the clock, including those shopping late at night or early in the morning.

The initiative comes as Remy Cointreau seeks to strengthen its position in China, where changing consumption habits and uneven demand across sales channels are reshaping the market for imported spirits.
The company's latest financial results suggest its digital strategy is gaining traction.

Remy Cointreau reported first-half fiscal 2026-27 sales of 510.9 million euros ($566.7 million), up 2.9 percent organically, according to the results released on Oct 28. Sales in the Asia-Pacific region rose 14.3 percent, supported by stronger shipments to China ahead of Mid-Autumn Festival and continued growth elsewhere in Asia.

Cognac sales in China increased at a high-single-digit rate in the first half, including mid-teens growth in the second quarter, Chief Financial Officer Luca Marotta said during the company's earnings presentation.

The recovery was uneven across distribution channels. Direct sales channels drove growth. E-commerce sales rose more than 30 percent in the second quarter and accounted for about 30 percent of China sales, according to Marotta.

Phe said the company has spent more than a decade building its e-commerce capabilities in China, including dedicated teams, customer relationship management systems and directly operated flagship stores on platforms such as Tmall and JD.

Operating its own online stores requires greater investment but provides more direct access to consumer data and allows the company to manage pricing and promotional campaigns more closely, she added.
The digital expansion is only one part of Remy Cointreau's response to changing Chinese drinking habits.
Chinese consumers are increasingly prioritizing quality over quantity, exploring different categories of spirits and seeking more personalized experiences, Phe said.
"They are not drinking more, but they are drinking better," she said. "For us, it's more about the value strategy than the volume strategy."

items.title: Europe weighs up US midterm power shift
text: Many Europeans were relieved when the Republican Party lost control of both chambers of the United States Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections, with the Democratic Party securing majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The elections followed almost two years of mounting strain in transatlantic ties that included Washington's tariff policies, its claims to Greenland, and repeated demands for more European defense spending.
The moves raised questions across Europe about the reliability of the US as an ally.

Differences between the US and Europe over the Russia-Ukraine crisis had added to the uncertainty surrounding Europe's security. Additionally, Europeans saw the US-Iran conflict as something that forced them to pay for US actions that disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and contributed to rising fuel prices and inflation, and an intensified cost-of-living crisis.

The Democratic Party's projected control of Congress could introduce stronger checks on the White House through legislative oversight, budgetary powers, and scrutiny of executive decisions. However, in the US political system, the president retains considerable authority over diplomacy and military operations, as well as certain tariff measures under powers delegated by Congress.
Against this backdrop, European policymakers and analysts are weighing up whether the change in the composition of Congress will make a difference to transatlantic ties.

While the Democrats' control of Congress could of fer some changes, analysts caution that things are unlikely to shift fundamentally when it comes to Washington's approach to Europe, and that it means there is unlikely to be a reversal in the continent's growing emphasis on strategic autonomy.

items.title: G7 repeats US falsehoods about Cuba: Cuban FM
text: HAVANA - Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Thursday that a recent Group of Seven (G7) statement ignored the harm caused by the US embargo against Cuba, while endorsing fabricated pretexts for punishing the Caribbean country.

In a post on the social media platform X, Rodriguez said the G7 foreign ministers' statement, released Wednesday after two days of talks in Paris, "omits the reality of the cruel impact of the blockade, the economic war and the energy blockade imposed by the US government against Cuba."
Rodriguez described US policy toward Cuba as "genocidal" and a "flagrant, massive and systematic" violation of the human rights of Cubans and the sovereignty of third countries.
He recalled that on Oct 28, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, which Washington has maintained for more than six decades.

Rodriguez said the international community had once again condemned the embargo at the General Assembly, while the G7 had chosen to repeat "false arguments fabricated by Washington" to justify the embargo.

The G7 members -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- expressed concern over Cuba's "profound economic crisis and humanitarian needs" and called for improvements in the delivery of humanitarian aid.

The statement's section on Cuba made no mention of the US embargo, economic sanctions or the Trump administration's threats of military intervention. It also did not address Washington's Jan 29 executive order, which set out a process for imposing additional tariffs on goods from countries that supply oil to Cuba.

items.title: Modernization rooted in Chinese cultural heritage
text: The selected works of President Xi Jinping on culture offer an insightful look at China's cultural policies.

Governing a country and explaining the theoretical underpinnings of its policies are two different things; in these writings, both are done — objectives are outlined, their foundations explained, and connections drawn to a broader societal vision.
Anyone aiming to understand China's developmental goals should examine the argument on its own terms, rather than evaluate it by its distance from Western models.
To begin with, let's define what cultural policy is. In France, it covers the arts, historic heritage, media and cultural industries.
However, in this book, it also encompasses the cultivation of shared values, the transmission of traditional culture, and the ideas that shape social life.
Its purpose is to help build a socialist society while preserving the continuity of Chinese civilization under the leadership of the Communist Party of China.
This involves decisions about educational content, the role of traditions, the values promoted through creative work and how traditional culture is interpreted.
In Xi's selected works, these elements are viewed as part of a unified effort to shape a society capable of pursuing common goals.
While economic development provides material resources, cultural policy shapes beliefs, knowledge and behavior, thereby influencing the kind of society China aspires to become.
This ambition leads to a central assertion: China can modernize without adopting Western norms.

A Western-centric perspective often assumes that countries become modern by gradually tilting toward Western societies. Their economies develop, their social attitudes change and their institutions eventually converge on Western-style democracy.
This view confuses transformation with an inevitable political destination.
Chinese modernization entails advancing science, enhancing industrial capabilities, raising living standards and adapting institutions to the country's needs.
Westernization, on the other hand, implies adopting Western political and cultural models as compulsory benchmarks. The two are distinct.
The book advocates learning from other cultures and adapting their contributions to Chinese circumstances.
The distinction is straightforward: a country can borrow a technology, an idea or a method without adopting every institution of the society that produced it.
Thus, the West no longer represents the future toward which every society must travel.
This plurality of paths is also relevant to BRICS nations, whose cooperation emphasizes sovereign equality and aims to promote a more representative international order.
This creates room to view development as more than just catching up with the West. While their trajectories differ, BRICS nations share no single modernization doctrine.
China's approach combines material progress, common prosperity and cultural development, distinguishing between the means of development and the societal goals they serve.

items.title: School bomb threats treated as hoaxes
text: Bomb threats sent to thousands of schools across the United Kingdom, Ireland and Italy are being treated as hoaxes by police — the latest in a wave of hoaxes and disruptions that have hit Europe in recent weeks.
Around 6,300 schools in Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threatening emails, according to local authorities.
Police in the Republic of Ireland said they were aware of a "generic communication" sent to a number of "educational establishments", but dismissed it as "not credible".

A number of schools in Italy were evacuated as a precaution, but Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks had so far found no evidence of "concrete danger". "These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.
A single email appears to have been sent on Wednesday to 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools, while private schools were unaffected, officials said.

Purporting to be from a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", the message caused alarm in many Italian schools. An email sent to Scottish schools, seen by the BBC, appeared to have similar wording and also referenced Mikhail Andropov — though as leader of a "Red Owl" project.
Police in Northern Ireland confirmed the email originated abroad and was being treated as a hoax.
Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said, "We take incidents of this nature very seriously, and we understand the concern in the community, school communities and for students and parents.
"Our inquiries are ongoing. However, at this stage, we consider the risk to the public as low."
Police Scotland said the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes, though several local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.
Scotland's Education Secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and that cybercrime specialists were hunting for whoever sent the messages.

Whether the incidents are linked remains unclear. Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara called them a probable "cyberattack, not a genuine risk", suggesting the wave of threats was a coordinated campaign.
The incidents have added to unease across the continent, which has seen a spate of disruptions including sabotage of supermarket refrigeration systems.
Last week, Italian airports and airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by bomb hoaxes that sparked evacuations.

items.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
text: An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.
The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.

items.title: How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
text: Editor’s note: Zhang Li is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Davis, and the author of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy,” which explores how a new psychotherapeutic culture is taking root in China amid profound socioeconomic change. A Chinese version of the book was released this summer. Here, Zhang, who grew up in Kunming, capital of the southwestern Yunnan province, talks with The Paper about her personal journey, trends in mental health care, and the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

The Paper: In your book, you say that returning home to Kunming to conduct research into the city’s mental and psychological landscape was a “deeply emotional experience” that sometimes left you feeling vulnerable. How did your personal connection with Kunming shape this project?

Zhang: The idea for the book first came to me when I learned that my best friend from middle school had become a therapist. I was quite surprised. This was around 2000, when interest in psychology was just beginning to take off in China and few people knew anything about mental health counseling. When I talked to my friend about her work, I realized that it touched on all kinds of everyday issues but was relatively unexplored. Most of the anthropological field research I’d come across had been conducted outside China.

As I worked on the project, I discovered how deeply it was connected to my family. My mother died 13 years ago. Looking back, I realized she’d lived with post-traumatic stress disorder for much of her life. She lost her mother when she was 8 years old. Her father remarried, and her stepmother treated her and her siblings very badly.

Growing up, we became accustomed to her extreme emotional reactions, but we had no idea they were symptomatic of a psychological disorder. Back then, people simply described this behavior as having “a bad temper.” It was only after reading up on the subject that I came to understand that my mother had suffered from chronic anxiety and depression, but she lacked the language to express it.

Seeing a psychiatrist is more normalized now; back then, mental health was a taboo topic. When I began my fieldwork, my mother was 80. I repeatedly urged her to see a psychiatrist, and eventually she agreed. After a complicated and rather haphazard diagnostic process, she was prescribed a short course of Prozac, which helped improve her condition. In the final three years of her life, she was relatively at peace, and we could have calmer, more constructive conversations.

I chose Kunming for my fieldwork because it allowed me to leverage personal connections and familiarity with the local environment. In addition, scholars were already conducting similar research in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, so I wanted to look at a medium-sized city. Kunming was experiencing many of the same problems as larger cities amid China’s economic reforms and social transformation. Rapid, large-scale change inevitably causes disruption, and the psychological disruption individuals experience manifests in all kinds of ways.

items.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
text: SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.
“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.
For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.

items.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
text: A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.
“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.
The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”
Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.
In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.
Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.
He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

items.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
text: Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.
But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.

items.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
text: “Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.
“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”
“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.
Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

items.title: Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo

text: SHANGHAI — The ninth China International Import Expo ran from Nov. 5 to 10, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 162 countries, regions and international organizations.

More than 480 exhibits made global, Asian or Chinese debuts. Qualcomm brought a 6G terminal prototype out of the lab. Medtronic’s China-developed Kanghui orthopedic surgical robot had its world premiere. And a rare type of durian tree fruit, the Malaysian white durian, made its global debut.

Robots at the expo could be found working hotel front desks, taking photos for visitors, and running booth demos on their own — visibly more advanced than in past years. In place of the mechanical arm designed to play ping-pong featured last year, at this year’s expo, a company debuted an entire humanoid robot playing the sport. At the forum held alongside the expo, Xiong Jijun, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology, said humanoid robots must be upgraded from performing simple actions to being “able to think and work.”
Sixth Tone photographers spent the week in the halls, capturing the new products, technologies and services on display.

items.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
text: The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.
The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

items.title: China's NEV exports surge 144.7% in Oct, growth expected to moderate as overseas markets mature
text: China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) exports surged 144.7 percent year-on-year in October, industry data showed on Monday, underscoring strong overseas demand even as domestic sales weakened. Industry analysts said that exports are likely to maintain robust momentum in the near term, although growth is likely to moderate as overseas markets mature and competition intensifies.

Chinese producers exported 582,000 passenger NEVs in October, up 3.9 percent from September, according to data released by the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). Meanwhile, domestic NEV retail sales fell 13.7 percent year-on-year to 1.109 million units, although they rose 2.3 percent month-on-month.
Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the CPCA, told the Global Times on Monday that China's automobile exports are expected to shift from rapid growth this year to a more moderate pace in 2027.

Cui forecast that overall vehicle export growth could slow to about 10 percent next year as shipments to Russia stabilize and exports to the EU face mounting pressure. The Middle East region could provide additional growth, although prospects remain uncertain, he said.
Passenger NEV exports reached 4.472 million units in the first 10 months of 2026, up 139.7 percent year-on-year, according to the CPCA.

These figures also point to a changing export structure. NEVs accounted for 62.8 percent of China's passenger vehicle exports in October, up 20 percentage points from a year earlier. Battery electric vehicles represented 61.7 percent of NEV shipments, while conventional plug-in hybrids accounted for 33.7 percent.

Leading Chinese automakers recorded substantial overseas shipments. BYD exported 165,194 passenger NEVs in October, followed by Chery with 83,843 and Geely with 80,119, CPCA figures showed. Tesla China's exports reached 59,012 units.

Zhang Xiang, a researcher at the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center of North China University of Technology, told the Global Times on Monday that Chinese automakers have established a competitive edge in the global NEV market through technological advances, mature supply chains and increasingly competitive products.

He said that he expects overseas demand to remain strong in the coming months, supporting continued export growth. However, as NEV adoption expands and initial demand is gradually absorbed, export growth is likely to return to a more sustainable pace over the longer term.

The expansion comes amid a changing international trade environment. The EU has imposed additional countervailing duties on China-made battery electric vehicles, while Chinese manufacturers are increasingly exploring emerging markets to diversify their overseas sales.

According to the International Energy Agency, sales of Chinese-made electric cars last year grew by 130 percent in Southeast Asia, 60 percent in the Middle East and 55 percent in Latin America, highlighting growing demand beyond traditional markets.

items.title: Singapore Business Federation leads 54 firms to CIIE to unlock bilateral and regional opportunities
text: Singapore firms continue to value China as an important market, and the Southeast Asian country's extensive business networks and familiarity with Southeast Asian markets make it a valuable partner for Chinese enterprises looking to expand their regional footprint, an executive of the Singapore Business Federation said.

China remains a significant market for Singapore businesses, underpinned by its vast consumer market, evolving demand and focus on high-quality development, Mark Lee, chairman of SBF, said during an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo held in Shanghai on Friday.

The federation is leading a delegation of 54 Singapore firms to the CIIE. Since the inaugural CIIE in 2018, Singapore businesses have generated about 2.79 billion yuan ($420 million) in cumulative trade value through the event.

Spanning established household names and emerging businesses, participating Singaporean firms at the expo highlight the country's competitive strength in food, health and wellness, consumer innovation, financial services and professional solutions.

They include See Hai Tat Medical Hall (Singapore) Pte Ltd, which looks to grow its consumer presence in China, and Prima Food Pte Ltd, which wants to use the CIIE to explore opportunities in the Chinese market.

With Singapore set to be the ASEAN chair in 2027, the SBF's participation in the CIIE this year — as it has done across all previous editions of the expo — further highlights its role as a strategic bridge for Chinese enterprises looking to expand into the ASEAN market, Lee said.

"Singapore features transparent, trusted legal frameworks and strong intellectual property protection, which helps safeguard technology rights as solutions expand into ASEAN and other regions. We are also a financing hub," Lee said, adding that this explains why many of the country's professional services partners are at the CIIE. They include banks, advisory firms, human resources consultants, legal service providers and trade compliance specialists.

He highlighted that China is among the global leaders in AI and digitization. Singaporean businesses want to work closely and conduct business with their Chinese counterparts, and such collaborations are already underway.

Lee raised the example of Pony.ai, a Chinese autonomous vehicle AI company, which partnered with ComfortDelGro, a Singaporean transport operator that runs taxi and fleet services. They launched a robotaxi pilot in China's Guangzhou, Guangdong province, and following the pilot, a robotaxi service was rolled out earlier this year in a designated area in Singapore, using Pony.ai's technology.

"ComfortDelGro stated that the pilot supports its broader global strategy covering China and Singapore, since it provides fleet management services across multiple markets. This illustrates a strong model: proven Chinese technology, localized by Singapore companies, with plans to scale into other regions and countries," Lee said.
Singapore and China share longstanding economic ties, with bilateral trade in goods reaching approximately 895.9 billion yuan last year

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Huang exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia

Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
text: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.

Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.

Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."

Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.

There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.

Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.

Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.

Jensen Huang Exit Sets Up US-China Showdown Over AI Chip Curbs
text: The fall of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has removed the industry’s most prominent opponent of US chip controls, setting up a showdown over potential new curbs that could accelerate China’s drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency.

Huang’s exit on Thursday smooths the way for lawmakers and the US Commerce Department to choke off China’s access to computing power through smuggling and other workarounds. Those measures, if enacted, risk provoking Beijing to retaliate and shattering a fragile truce reached by Donald Trump and Xi Jinping over their cordial summits.

items.title: ‘End of an era’: Jensen Huang’s abrupt exit stuns Nvidia’s China staff
Nvidia scandal: Howard Lutnick under pressure over alleged lack of action
text: US commerce secretary faces sack as warnings emerge about alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang and delays in adding Megaspeed to trade blacklist
Analysis: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
One of Donald Trump’s top lieutenants reportedly could soon be fired, as criticism mounts over commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer, Colette Kress, after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Pressure is mounting on Lutnick after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.
Lutnick is scheduled to testify alongside the ousted Nvidia chief before Congress in the coming weeks.

He is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.
White House officials are now discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported.

John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”.

Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls” and that: “Heads should roll.”

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.

Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.

On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.

items.title: Why Singapore keeps turning up in the fight over Nvidia chips and China
text: Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.

The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country.

A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday.

Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.
The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development.

Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.
Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up.

Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year.
Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering.

Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
text: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.
Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.
"The American people deserve answers," he added.
Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.
Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
